Overall, quarterly revenue of $3.74 billion came in just below LSEG estimates of $3.75 billion. "We're really proud of the print, and we're going to keep building for the long term and ignore the noise day to day," Finkelstein said. Subscription revenue of $836 million also missed analyst estimates of $848.1 million, according to FactSet. Merchant revenue beat estimates. The software company saw a slowdown in U.S. commercial total contract value growth. Apple shares also sank as the company reckons with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. In this article AAPL PLTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:00 02:00 Palantir's CEO on Q3 results and boom in company's commercial business Morning Call Palantir shares fell on Tuesday after the software company reported third-quarter earnings and analysts pointed to signs of a slowdown in total contract value and other "forward indicators." U.S. commercial revenue topped government for the first time, but the company closed $1.5 billion in TCV in the segment, up 11% from last year. In Q2, Palantir closed a record $2.1 billion worth of TCV in the segment, which was up 153% from the prior year. Investors will "no doubt be looking for evidence in subsequent quarters that 11% growth in U.S. commercial TCV bookings is a fluke of duration and not something structural," a Piper Sandler note from Monday said. "We believe that is the case and demand for PLTR's solutions still very much outstrip supply." In a Tuesday note, Goldman Sachs analysts noted that the company attributed some of this to shorter contract durations. "The key will be converting shorter duration contracts into longer duration commitments, which Palantir has done successfully in the past," the analysts wrote. Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time, Palantir said in its earnings report. Palantir stock chart. Apple's earnings The iPhone maker reported better-than-expected revenue in its fourth-quarter earnings, but fell short of estimates on iPad sales and issued a margin forecast that disappointed investors. Apple 's statement marked the first earnings report since John Ternus took over as CEO from Tim Cook in September. The stock fell more than 2% on Tuesday. The company is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. Memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period, the company said Monday. Despite the price surge, Ternus said Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." He told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "The concern is profitability," said Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares. "Management pointed to memory as the main pressure, together with the cost of rolling out Siri AI. Memory shortages are also expected to limit Mac and iPad supply, as demand has run ahead of plans." Apple shares have risen 25% in 2026, ahead of other big tech names, but that premium leaves "little room for disappointment," Todorova added. Joe Burbank | Tribune News Service | Getty Images Disney is planning to cut several thousand jobs, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. Some managers at the entertainment giant have been asked to reduce costs by up to 20%, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. It marks the latest round of layoffs since CEO Josh D'Amaro took the reins earlier this year. The update comes after separate plans in April to cut as many as 1,000 employees , predominantly in the marketing department, and in September to cut about 300 employees , many in human resources and technology divisions. Bloomberg was first to report the latest round of layoffs. Company executives warned of the possibility of more reductions in its August earnings report. "We remain highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise to create incremental capacity to invest for growth and are evaluating a variety of levers," D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston wrote in an Aug. 5 letter to shareholders . "We are mid-stream in this work and will provide future updates on our progress." Disney introduced plans in August for an early retirement program for some employees. "This is one of several actions we're taking to reshape our organization, including involuntary staff reductions that have already begun in some areas and will continue into next year," Chief People Officer Sonia Coleman wrote in a letter to employees on Aug. 24. Disney had about 231,000 employees as of the close of its fiscal year 2025, which ended in September of that year, according to the company's annual financial report. Disney is not the only entertainment company looking to reduce costs. Netflix said in a memo last month that it would lay off roughly 6% of its workforce . Skydance , the newly combined company of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is also expected to cut staff in an effort to realize $6 billion in synergies over three years. headlines.article_text: Yum Brands (YUM) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Yum Brands beat Wall Street's quarterly earnings estimates and its revenue was in line with expectations. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined as a cyclospora outbreak tied to lettuce served at its restaurants weighed on traffic. During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. In this article YUM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A woman leaving Taco Bell on July 28, 2026, in Washington,DC. The Washington Post | Getty Images Yum Brands on Tuesday reported earnings that beat expectations, but a cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell weighed on the company's same-store sales growth. However, Yum said Taco Bell, which the company considers a "growth engine" for its business, has since rebounded. "Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth," Yum CEO Chris Turner said in a statement. Taco Bell's same-store sales are up about 1% so far in the fourth quarter, CFO Ranjith Roy said on the company's earnings conference call Tuesday. In the last four weeks ended Friday, same-store sales have risen 3% compared with the year-ago period. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.56 adjusted vs. $1.49 expected Revenue: $2.05 billion vs. $2.05 billion expected Yum reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $1.62 billion, or $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, or $1.41 per share, a year earlier. Excluding gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut and other items, the restaurant company earned $1.56 per share. Net sales rose 4% to $2.05 billion. During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. It closed the sale of the pizza chain's business in mainland China to Yum China on Aug. 7 and sold the rest of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. The company's third-quarter results include Pizza Hut up until those dates. Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum's same-store sales were flat for the quarter as Taco Bell weighed on the company's overall results. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined by 4% as diners temporarily pulled back on visits due to the foodborne illness outbreak . Yum executives previously said the weekend of July 18 saw the most severe impact to sales, but trends have improved since then. Taco Bell's most loyal customers returned faster, Yum said, thanks in part to weekly Tuesday deals for loyalty program members after the cyclospora outbreak took over headlines. Traffic from "medium" and "light" customers has bounced back to about 95% of prior levels, while visits from "heavy" users is back to normal, Roy said. To attract more casual diners, Taco Bell has been relying on star power, like a collaboration with pop star Olivia Rodrigo on a pink-colored Mountain Dew Baja Blast. Outside of the U.S., Taco Bell's much smaller international business reported same-store sales growth of 5%. KFC's same-store sales ticked up 1%, helped by system sales growth in China and Europe. The U.S., now the chicken chain's third-largest market, saw system sales shrink 6% in the quarter. Like Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes , KFC has struggled in the U.S. amid a wave of new competitors and more budget-conscious consumers. Its home market represents only about 5% of KFC's operating profit, but it remains a symbolically important part of the business for Yum investors. During the quarter, KFC U.S. launched popcorn chicken, which sold out in many restaurants. However, Yum said the limited-time menu item was not enough to offset the successful Hot & Spicy Wings and Potato Wedges promotion during the year-ago period. Globally, KFC is trying to become "the most modern chicken QSR ," Turner said on the company's earnings conference call. To achieve that lofty goal, he said the chain will roll out buzzy promotions, a new brand identity, and a wider menu that includes upgraded sauces and more beverages. headlines.article_text: Bill Ackman warns of 'casino' stock market trading Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ackman says the volatility has also created opportunities for Pershing Square to buy companies it considers high quality at discounted prices. Ackman points to Microsoft, Amazon, Visa, Mastercard and Netflix while warning that short-term speculation can hurt investors. Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box on Nov. 3rd, 2026. CNBC Bill Ackman worries that the stock market is broken, saying the rise of speculative trading is leading to wild price swings thanks to the amount of leverage in the system. "Every number of days, I feel like markets are broken," Ackman told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Tuesday. "Stocks trade at prices that make no sense to me. Yes, it's good if you're a long-term investor and you can buy at a stupid price. I don't think it's good for the country generally." "We're back to the casino type markets when there was 95% leverage," he added. "I don't think that's inherently good for the economy, for society, and it's leading to these massive moves in stocks." The founder of Pershing Square Capital Management said those same dislocations in the market have given the hedge fund the opportunity to snag big bargains. watch now VIDEO 5:16 05:16 I don't see roaring 1920s comparison in the stock market: Bill Ackman Squawk Box Pershing bought Microsoft , for example, when it was pummeled during the "SaaSpocalypse" earlier this year, and Amazon when it fell following President Donald Trump's tariffs. It also bought Alphabet when the stock moved "massively" following ChatGPT's launch, he said. But the billionaire investor worries that the rise of one-day leveraged vehicles, perpetual futures and sports betting is dangerous for investors who are treating the stock market as a get-rich-quick scheme — an attitude that could have disastrous consequences. "It's good for us long term, us being Pershing Square," he said. "I don't think it's good for the country." Among the stocks Ackman is especially bullish on are Visa and Mastercard , which he called among the world's "greatest" businesses, as well as streaming platform Netflix, in which he disclosed a position in August. headlines.article_text: Apple earnings: John Ternus faces first test amid high memory costs Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points In John Ternus' first earnings report as CEO, Apple issued a gross margin forecast that disappointed Wall Street, sending the stock down after hours. Apple blamed higher memory prices and some costs related to Siri AI for the shrinking margins. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," Ternus said. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Apple CEO John Ternus delivers a keynote address during the Apple Experience LA event in Los Angeles, California, on Oct. 28, 2026, introducing new Mac computer models. Frederic J. Brown | AFP | Getty Images John Ternus' first earnings report as Apple CEO was going fine until it was time to issue a forecast for the company's gross margin, one of the key metrics followed by investors. Apple reported better-than-expected earnings and revenue on Monday, including in the company's core iPhone unit, and even projected sales in the current period that topped estimates. But just before Ternus opened the earnings call up to analysts' questions, CFO Kevan Parekh came forward with the first real piece of bad news. Parekh said that for the December quarter, which goes through the holiday season, Apple's gross margin will be between 45% and 46%, trailing the 46.3% average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. "This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI," Parekh said. Apple shares slid 3% in morning trading on Tuesday. Apple stock chart It's part of an ongoing trend for Apple, which is absorbing some of the soaring costs from the global memory shortage. A margin drop in the fiscal first quarter would be a third straight decline for Apple, following a gross margin of 50.1% in the June period and 47.9% in the September quarter, boosted by 1 percentage point of tariff refunds. At the midpoint of the forecast range, it would be Apple's lowest gross margin since the fiscal fourth quarter of 2023. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus said on the call, adding that the company is paying more than it did earlier this year. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase." Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, is grappling with a problem that his predecessor spent his final months addressing. Cook told The Wall Street Journal in June that the memory situation was a "hundred-year flood." Apple followed by raising prices across the board on Macs, iPads and accessories. In September, Apple increased the prices of its iPhones by $100, which Ternus said the company did "reluctantly." 'Less flexibility in the supply chain' Computer and smartphone makers everywhere are suffering. On Friday, Intel had its worst day on the market since the 1970s due to a weak forecast tied to the softening PC market. It's all because of insatiable artificial intelligence demand. AI server giants like Nvidia and hyperscalers are buying up all the RAM they can find, and they're willing to pay a premium for it, leaving little supply for companies that make smartphones and tablets. Despite its size and global clout, Apple said it expects supply constraints on iPhones and Macs in the holiday quarter, primarily driven by memory. On the call, Ternus had some top lieutenants field component-related questions. Sabih Khan, chief operating officer, became the first Apple COO to appear on an earnings call since Cook in 2010, when Steve Jobs was CEO. "As we have said before, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal," Khan told analysts on the call. watch now VIDEO 4:06 04:06 Apple's shares remain attractive over the next 12 months, says Neuberger's Flax Squawk Box Asia In response, Apple has drastically increased its purchase obligations to secure supply, Khan said. Those obligations rose by $33 billion from the June quarter to the September period, Khan said, though he declined to answer questions about whether Apple had signed "long-term agreements" with memory makers. "We're always working hard to improve supply," Khan said. Even with the recent margin slide, Apple's gross margins are still well above where they sat earlier in the Cook era, when the number would predictably come in between 38% and 39%. As Apple's profitable services business grew, its gross margin expanded , hitting 40% in 2021 and growing from there. Analysts see a potential silver lining for Apple in the current market turmoil. Because Apple is more capable of eating a portion of the increased costs, some experts predict the company will take market share from makers of Windows PC and Android phones that don't have such a cushion. Citing data from a third-party researcher, Ternus said gains are already happening. "According to IDC, we gained share globally for the quarter and for the full fiscal year," Ternus said. "And we have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time, which is a truly remarkable testament to these incredible products."
